title: Frontend rendering & state
summary: Server-side vs client-side rendering, what 'state' means on the client, keeping server and client data in sync, and how a Java backend serves each model.
note:
1. SSR: server builds HTML per request; fast first paint, more server work
2. CSR: browser fetches JSON and renders; rich interactivity, slower first paint
3. State = the data the UI renders from (server data + local UI data)
4. Keep a single source of truth and sync carefully to avoid stale views

recall.q: SSR vs CSR in one trade-off?
recall.a: SSR gives a faster first paint and better SEO at more server cost; CSR gives richer interactivity but a slower initial load.
The data the UI currently renders from — both a cache of server data and local-only bits like form input or which tab is open.

recall.q: Main risk when the client caches server data?
recall.a: Staleness — the cached copy drifts from the server; you reconcile with refetching, cache invalidation, or optimistic updates.

shot.title: SSR vs CSR
shot.body:
| | SSR | CSR |
|---|---|---|
| HTML built | on server | in browser |
| first paint | fast | slower |
| SEO | strong | needs work |
| server load | higher | lower |
| interactivity | page reloads | in-place updates |

sections.title: SSR vs CSR
sections.body: ✍️ **Server-side rendering** builds the full HTML on each request (classic Thymeleaf/JSP, or Next.js): quick first paint, SEO-friendly, but the server does the work every time. **Client-side rendering** ships a JS bundle that fetches JSON and renders in the browser: a slower first load but snappy, app-like interaction afterward. Many apps mix both (hydration).

sections.title: What client state is
sections.body:
✍️ 'State' is just the data the UI draws from. Two kinds: **server state** (a cached copy of data the backend owns) and **local UI state** (form text, open menus, selected tab). Keeping them separate and having one **source of truth** prevents the UI from showing contradictory things.
- Rule of thumb: derive what you can; store only what you must.

sections.title: Keeping them in sync
sections.body: ✍️ The hard part is staleness: the browser's copy drifts from the server. Reconcile by refetching on focus, invalidating a cache after a mutation, or doing **optimistic updates** (show the change immediately, roll back if the server rejects it). The REST contract (status codes, idempotent retries) is what makes this safe.
